q: tell me about the French Revolution
a: The French Revolution (1789-1799) was a period of profound social and political upheaval in France that overthrew the monarchy, established a republic, and fundamentally reshaped modern European history. It began in 1789 due to a combination of factors: massive national debt from France's involvement in the American Revolution, widespread food shortages and rising bread prices, an outdated feudal system that burdened the common people (the Third Estate) while exempting the nobility and clergy from taxes, and Enlightenment ideas about liberty, equality, and popular sovereignty. Key events included the convening of the Estates-General in May 1789, the Tennis Court Oath (June 20, 1789), the Storming of the Bastille on July 14, 1789 (now France's national holiday), and the Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen in August 1789. The Revolution became more radical in 1792-1794 during the Reign of Terror led by Maximilien Robespierre and the Committee of Public Safety, when tens of thousands of perceived enemies of the revolution were executed by guillotine. King Louis XVI and Queen Marie Antoinette were executed in 1793. The Revolution eventually ended with Napoleon Bonaparte's coup d'état in 1799, leading to the Napoleonic era. The French Revolution had enormous global impact: it spread nationalist and democratic ideals across Europe, ended feudalism in France, established the metric system, inspired revolutionary movements in Haiti and Latin America, and fundamentally changed how people thought about government, citizenship, and human rights.
